utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. May I remind you, Mr. Radic, of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Can we please briefly go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, yesterday we got as far as the 20th of November, 1991. Let us try not to repeat everything you talked about yesterday. You told us where you spent some of that time and before you were off to your regular briefing, where else did you go on that day -- or rather, having left the Danube Hotel, did you go anywhere else at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's one thing that I would like to say again just to link-up with yesterday's testimony. After leaving the hospital, I started moving back towards the down-town area. I went back to the Vupik cellar and then proceeded to the down-town area, where I stayed in the hotel for a while. I remember wanting to climb up to the upper floors of the Danube Hotel so that I could gain a vantage point, an elevation from which I would have an open view of the town that had been destroyed. Having spent some time at the Danube Hotel, I walked back down the axis of operations of my company to the area in which I was normally staying at, Nova Street. I got the impression at this time that the soldiers whom I had given orders to that morning to inspect the route and collect all combat and non-combat equipment found along the route had done their work very thoroughly. I don't remember coming across a single piece of equipment, a single weapon, a single case of ammunition, grenades, or any other sort of ordnance which was of paramount importance to me at this point in time. Having reached Nova Street, I lingered there until I was off to our regular briefing at the headquarters of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Who attended this regular briefing and did you receive any assignments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the command members were there as well as the company commanders of the 1st Battalion. At the briefing we heard that, over the course of the following morning, the commander, Major Tesic, would go to a reception organised by the federal secretary. He showed us a camouflage uniform that he had received, which I had already had the previous day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if Captain Stijakovic was there, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I remember is that they were both present at one point in time. A little later -- I seem to remember Major Tesic was off somewhere. Perhaps he had imparted some brief orders and was then off to prepare. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when the meeting eventually drew to a close?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the principal orders given at the meeting was about the fact that Captain Stijakovic had taken over command responsibility for the following period of time while the commander was absent. The order was for the following morning to prepare our companies so that he might attend a review of troops so that he could check the condition and physical appearance of all the soldiers, that being one of the tasks. This was one of the steps taken by the command to bring order back to the unit, both in terms of discipline and in terms of the sort of physical appearance normally required from soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. After this, where else did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just before the meeting ended, we officers talked among ourselves. Second Lieutenant Vuckovic called us, other commanders, to come for dinner over to his place, because, as far as I remember, one of the locals from his own neighbourhood had roasted a pig and he wanted to have us over for dinner. As far as I remember, Zoran Zirojevic and I ended up going. I can't remember, but I think Captain Kopcic was not there or Captain Sasa Bojkovski for that matter. I remember that I meant to do something for his benefit and the benefit of his soldiers, so I left the command post and went back to Nova Street because I still had some cartons of cigarettes left there. I grabbed one of those to take back to Second Lieutenant Vuckovic and his soldiers. A little later I reached a street that was called Oslobodjenje Street; this was at the top of Petrova Gora. As far as I remember, I was met there by one of Lieutenant Vuckovic's soldiers, who then took me to a house. I think it was still being built and the walls had not been white-washed yet. I remember us staying in a rather large room, which I believed at the time to be the living-room. We sat there at a table -- or rather, it was several tables put together for the occasion, and we sat down on benches and chairs --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was seated next to Lieutenant Vuckovic. Next to us -- or rather, facing us across the table there may have been Captain Zirojevic. There were other soldiers there from Vuckovic's own unit as well as some locals, I think, but I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I won't ask you about the food and drinks. The OTP perhaps might want to know, so they should ask. How long did you stay there for and where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That evening we managed to relax somewhat. We knew by this time that the war was now over and it had been a very difficult time. We exchanged stories, each from our own respective areas. In a way, we were exchanging jokes. We were trying to relax. We were there until just before daybreak. I can't remember specifically what time it was when I left, but I had some trouble igniting the engine of my car because it was bitterly cold and it took quite some time. Something had frozen inside the car, and I took some time trying to remove the ice so I could drive back to the house where I was sleeping at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you sleep that particular night? You remember the ground-plan we were looking at yesterday. Do you remember the specific room in that house in which you slept that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- rather, yes. The previous day Stanko Vujanovic's sister had left the hospital compound. I now knew that she was in Stanko Vujanovic's house, or rather, their father's house. I arrived very late, and this is why I didn't want to go to the large house in which I normally slept but rather I spent the night -- I spent the night in the smaller house, which is what I sometimes did from time to time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you perhaps remember something - and I'm sure you've had your memory refreshed over the years - do you remember what happened the next day? Did you have any assignments that you had received on the previous day? Were you carrying these out? What happened when you woke up, in one word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that I found it very difficult to get up that day. I had lost sight of the fact, so to speak, to the fact that Captain Stijakovic had ordered a review for the following day. I know someone came over to wake me up. I know that eventually I rose and the company had already assembled at the near end of Nova Street. I went to review and I can't remember every single thing that Captain Stijakovic checked, but one thing I do remember is we did our best throughout that time to behave as we normally would have back in the barracks. After just under two months at the front line - and this applied equally to everyone, the foot soldiers and me as their company commander - we faced situations every day where we had to make our own independent calls. So this situation struck me as somewhat strange at the time because it now appeared that we were going back to normal, something that we had totally forgotten about during the fighting. I can't remember exactly how long the review took, but I suppose it must have been something between half an hour and an hour. This wasn't just for checking; this was also for the purpose of socialising with a soldier, having a chat, familiarising himself with the situation, what have we done, what have we not done yet, what remains to be done, that sort of thing. After the review, to be quite frank, I could hardly wait to get this over with so that I could go back to my room and get some rest, some rest that I very badly needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean that you went back to sleep or just to get some rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where Captain Stijakovic went after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He went to visit one of the companies. I don't recall whether it was the 1st or the 2nd Company, I can't recall now, but I think that it was the 2nd Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At this review, were all the soldiers from your company present except for those that had been wounded or in hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The basic objective of the review was for the battalion command to see for themselves what the situation was at the time, because in this period, in those days, there were rumours circulating among us that the unit should continue with combat activities on the axis leading towards the town of Osijek. All of us were exhausted, and we literally prayed to God for the command to reach the decision that we should all go back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now if you would be so kind, tell us whether all the soldiers were in uniforms, regular army uniforms, or whether anyone was dressed in any other way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the last few days before this event, I personally issued a task to Second Lieutenant Hadzic and the company officer, commanding officer, to take all the measures necessary for the soldiers to look as soldiers should. During the combat activities, in fact, I personally took great efforts and I never allowed any of my soldiers to appear before me pretending that he was, I don't know what. They all had to have a soldierly appearance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the review, was this Spasoje Petkovic, a soldier by the name of Spasoje Petkovic present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the soldiers were present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, fine. Let me now go back to the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion. My question is: When you get your task and the plans from the commander, Tesic, you, the commanders of the regular companies of the 1st Motorised Battalion, you get your orders from Tesic. And would you agree that this is what you stated yesterday, that the Territorial Defence got their orders and plans related to the coordination of their activities from Tesic and Jaksic. Is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour. Your Honour, that's a very leading question. He can ask who he got orders from. This is in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, that's very well-founded, as you know. What you put to the witness then was not a repeat of the evidence he gave yesterday, it was some of your own evidence and on a very important point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not like to get into an argument. This was Radic's statement, that was his testimony, and I wanted to merely go back to his statement and refer to it, but okay. I accept the ruling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued orders to you, the company commanders, the next day? I'm just trying to make things simple; that's what I'm asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In all the situations in combat from the very first day until the very last moment that we spent, that my company spent there in the Vukovar area, I only and exclusively received my orders from battalion commander, Major Tesic. In certain situations, I received orders from his deputy, Major -- I'm sorry, Captain Stijakovic, Slavko Stijakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then when you went to the observation post - you talked about that yesterday - did you then make some special sketches based on those tasks and plans when you were on your own and when you were trying to elaborate those plans. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every commander, when he receives a task from his superior commander, he then engages in a certain mental process in which he has to comprehend the essence of this task. He had to grasp the idea and the objective that his commander had in mind. He then makes an assessment of the situation in terms of time and space, and then he makes his own decision on the manner in which the combat mission is going to be carried out. This rule is something that exists. This is something that I was taught in military school, and there is no other way in which a subordinate commanding officer can act, no other procedure that he can follow, once he has received his task from his superior. I think that this is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you elaborate the tasks and the plans you received from Commander Tesic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who issues tasks and plans at the command post to the Territorial Defence, to the leaders or commanders of the Territorial Defence detachments? That's what I mean. Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we heard a witness here; he was the commander of the staff and a detachment of the Territorial Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to this, Your Honour. This is non-responsive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Carry on, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not attend the situations where orders were issued by the detachment commander, the TO detachment commander, because there was no need for me to attend those meetings. The coordination and cooperation was something that was organised by the commanders, and we, the subordinates, we simply implemented it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the field, do you command the 3rd Company, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Miroljub Vujovic command the Territorial Defence units and the members of the 3rd Assault group in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic commanded the unit of the Territorial Defence. Now, whether it was a company or a detachment, I never actually needed to know that nor was I at all interested in this issue. But he commanded this -- the troops along the same axis where my unit, my company, was deployed with the Territorial Defence unit up until the time when he was wounded, which is on the 5th of November, and after the 14th of November when he returned to Vukovar. The Leva Supoderica unit, from the first to the last moment when the Leva Supoderica unit reached the axis of operation of the 3rd Motorised Company was under the command of Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni. The assault group --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We heard all about that, the axis of operation. What I wanted to know is who commanded them. The second question: 10th of November, 1991, Milovo Brdo. You were present in court when an order was exhibited dated 14th of November, 16th of November, 20th of October, and so on by General Mile Mrksic, so issued by General Mile Mrksic. So my question to you is: When you took Milovo Brdo and when, according to your evidence, three companies remained there at Milovo Brdo, did your one have its own axis of operation - and now we will not go back to what was heard about the 1st Motorised Battalion - I wanted to know who commanded the JOD 1, what troops were there, and who was there after you left Milovo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me correct you here. So it is not correct to say that three companies remained at Milovo Brdo. The 3rd Company remained there, the 2nd Company was in some kind of a reserve, so to speak, because it was the smallest in size and they mostly received tasks from the commander to secure certain facilities that had already been liberated. Now, as for the 1st Company, it was in the Pionirsko Naselje part of the town, and it went to the 1st of May Street all the way up to the textile school. So it is not correct to say that all three companies were at Milovo Brdo; only my company was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your correction. What about JOD 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of a meeting with a battalion commander, after the 10th of October, Major Tesic, the battalion commander --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about October or November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: November. I do apologise. So the battalion commander, Major Tesic, told us that all the members of the Territorial Defence, that all members of the Leva Supoderica units, and that all the volunteers in their units had to provide support to the 2nd Assault Detachment by moving to an axis and that they would be under the command of Major Tesic. Now, I know that at one point they left Milovo Brdo and they continued fighting towards -- going towards the city centre, towards the workers' hall, the Danube Hotel, and that on the 7th of November, they actually -- the 17th of November, they actually did get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt until he finished his answer. Your Honour, this is outside of the summary for this witness. Yesterday I didn't object to at least two or three occasions when matters were outside of the summary. Again, it's outside of the summary. We've received no notice of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Stanko Vujanovic at any point on the axis of operation of your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now tell the Court where he was, on which axis of operation during this whole operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unit commanded by Miroljub Vujovic was in the same area where I was, on the same axis. And from what I know, Stanko Vujanovic was on the axis of the 1st Motorised Company, which was itself commanded by Sasa Bojkovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And Stanko Vujanovic in the course of combat, did he actually sleep in his father's house where you had your operation post or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can state with full responsibility that he did not. Stanko Vujanovic was on the axis of the 1st Motorised Company at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean that he had no reason to discuss anything with you and to arrange anything with you regarding your axis of operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not have any reason at any time whatsoever with regard to combat activities to say a single word to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Radic, you probably remember we heard in court that on the 20th of November, 1991, you allegedly sent three soldiers to Ovcara. You did not mention this in your statement, in your evidence. What is your opinion on this statement that was made here in court? You yourself were here, you heard it; I'm not going to now recount what was said. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This statement was strange to me, to say the least. Were the situation not serious, I would even go as far as to say it was ridiculous because it was made by a person that I had spent a lot of time with, invested a lot of my time with the very best of intentions, primarily in an effort to make this person see that his priority task had been to survive. And I can now state with full responsibility that at that time I did not have a single reason whatsoever that I did not need at all to send any of my soldiers to a site where I had never been, either before or after. And at that time, I did not know at all that any activities were going on at Ovcara. I would like to also corroborate this with the following fact. I believed -- and had I been told or informed about any kind of event, I would have gone to that place myself; I wouldn't have sent a soldier in my place. Had I been convinced that there was any need for my unit to go there or any of my soldiers to go there, I would have sought permission for that from my superior command, the battalion commander, or his deputy. I cannot say, but it was a big surprise for me, especially because I hoped that the person who talked about that would tell the real truth. I was satisfied in some way that he would testify -- when I heard that he would testify, but I'm actually very surprised by what he actually said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. That person, who is a protected witness in this case, mentioned the presence of soldier Vidacek and a person by the name of Dzankovic. Did you know this older person, Dzankovic, and did he come to you to the observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I have been in this courtroom for a long time, I will say that witness P022 during his testimony made up two persons who allegedly went with him to Ovcara. Both of those people are dead. I am not in a position to confront any one of those people, but I assert that soldier Vidacek did not go with witness P022. And I would particularly not send Dzankovic because I never exchanged a single word with that man. I knew who he was. I used to see him around when I was in Vukovar, but I didn't know anything about that man. And to send him with two of my soldiers to a place where I didn't know what was going on is something that I would -- that would have never crossed my mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And would Dzankovic and Vidacek be able to confirm the statement of P022? Do you know what happened to those two people? If you were asked that, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was still in active service in early 1992, I received information that soldier Vidacek was killed in Zenica. I tried to check this information, but I wasn't successful. As for Dzankovic, I know that he activated an anti-tank grenade. He didn't know, actually, how to operate that, and that's how he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that witness P022 cannot confirm what he said in his testimony and nobody who is alive can confirm that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's argumentative and it's very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it is of no weight, whatever it is, Mr. Weiner. Thank you. It's a matter for your address, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, did you ever physically abuse your soldiers or any other soldier in the area of Vukovar? What is your position? What was your attitude towards the soldiers who were in combat at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yesterday I tried to explain to Their Honours and to all the parties in the courtroom that I personally believe that I put in all of my human and professional qualities for the purpose of protecting and assisting all those present on the axis of the 3rd Motorised Company. If anyone ever saw me behaving in a non-professional, unprofessional manner, I would like them to come forward and tell the Court about it. Only once was I in a situation where in attempting to save my own reputation, the reputation of an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army to react personally, this was on the 5th of October when there was an unsuccessful attempt to bring out the body of Vostic, Radoje, who had been killed. The house where I was with a number of soldiers who were also trying to help me was also the place where at that point there was a reservist who had arrived with my company from Belgrade. His name was mentioned in this courtroom before; his last name is Krstic. And on that occasion he attacked me verbally, saying that I was an unfit officer, that he did not want to be under the command of officers -- commanding officers who were unfit, and that all of them - thinking of the soldiers - would be killed by the enemy side, and that he did not want to continue to fight anymore. Since there were some other members of my company from the reserve forces and also some regular soldiers and in order to defend my honour and the honour of officers of the Yugoslav People's Army, I personally disarmed Private Krstic and asked the others present, those from the reserves, whether any one of them shared the opinion of Krstic. Two other reservists spoke up. They were not undisciplined. They also said that they didn't want to fight any longer either. And I had sent witness P022 to the command post, the -- where the battalion commander was. There was a platoon of military police at that command post under the command of Lieutenant Predrag Stefanovic at the time, second lieutenant. And I had requested the commander to send some military policemen, who would then escort these three reservists to the command. I state with full responsibility that in my presence no one laid a finger on those soldiers, and I know also that after speaking with them, the commander sent them to Negoslavci, where they were on guard duty guarding the motor vehicles that were at Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Your explanation was longer than necessary. We have to keep time in mind. At the command post of the 1st Motorised Battalion, that room where the command held its meetings, was that someplace that soldiers who were escorting you could enter? Could they attend those meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If soldiers happened to be in the -- on the personal security of the commander, there was a yard with the house where the command of the battalion was situated. On the left side of that house was a small room; we called it a summer kitchen. And all the soldiers could go in there to be warm so that they wouldn't have to wait outside for their commander. The house itself had a soldier posted in front of the door, so nobody could enter that building without permission of the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you heard and you probably met (redacted) (redacted). Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never had the opportunity to meet the gentleman face-to-face. I never exchanged a single word with him in my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You heard talk about him being in Vukovar. Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the first moment --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think maybe we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness P022 claims that he was your courier. Can you explain that person's role and his assignments in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness P022 was a courier of the commander of the 1st Platoon that was attached to the company commander in the early days of combat operations performed by my company. My courier was a soldier whose name I mentioned at the outset who hailed from Zagreb. Witness P022 was the courier of the commander of the 1st Platoon. All platoon commanders sent their couriers to the company commander at my request or when requested by those same platoon commanders. On the 10th of October, when I was hit and taken to the Negoslavci hospital, upon my return to our axis of operations - and I had been driven to Negoslavci by witness P022 of all people - in a yard outside which I had been hit myself, I found six wounded -- or rather, five wounded and one dead soldier. This dead soldier was a member of the 3rd Motorised Company and the only soldier to be killed during the fighting in Vukovar. He was also the signals officer in my company. There was the RUP-12 radio that he was carrying. This radio had been hit and damaged by a mortar shell. This was the main reason for the battalion command to decide that all company commanders and platoon commanders would be given Motorolas to use so that they would have better communications equipment over the course of the operations. Once the fighting was over, there was no need for me to send couriers anywhere because I had a line of communication that was both safe and reliable. It would indeed have been a very strange decision for me to take in addition to having this Motorola, which is a state-of-the-art piece of communication equipment, to use a courier in addition to this, especially since I knew that radios were the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an error in the transcript. He said he had no need to send couriers anywhere since he had no Motorolas and the transcript says: "Once the fighting was over." So can this please be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It needs to be clarified what the witness was saying, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please be so kind as to explain when the need ceased to send out couriers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldier Djordje Nikolic died on the 10th of November. I can't specifically remember if this was on the next day or two or three days later -- the 10th of October. The 10th of October is when Nikolic died. I'm sorry if I made a slip of the tongue. After that, the battalion command distributed to all its subordinate units the required number of Motorolas. The TO staff command distributed to all TO commanders the same type of equipment so that we all had Motorolas in our system of communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, but I think you forget the first part of my question. What about witness P022 and witness Vidacek, were they part of your security in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to go back to something briefly. From that moment on, I did not have any couriers, nor did I need any for that matter. Therefore, neither witness P022 nor Dragan Vidacek were my couriers or part of my escort. All I can say is over the first 15 or 20 days of my time there, I had gained sufficient self-confidence as an officer to enable me, after about a fortnight, to go to the service facilities at Petrova Gora and I got a motor vehicle issued to me there that I was using. And I no longer had anyone else escorting me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness P018, you were in the courtroom then, weren't you? He also says that he was your courier. Which precise assignments did he have as a member of your company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unlike witness P022, who was an arrogant soldier, he was undisciplined but he was exceptionally capable. So unlike him, witness P018 was such a poor soldier that I, as his commander, was in no position to entrust him with even the simplest of tasks. At one point in time he claimed to have cleaned my boots; I simply don't remember that. I don't remember ever ordering anyone to clean my boots; however, I claim with full responsibility and without meaning to slight anyone that this man was a soldier fit only for that type of assignment and nothing more. I would never have dispatched him to combat simply because I would never believe that he would be safe. At one point in time when we were at Nova Street, he left for Sava Kovacevica Street in the middle of combat at his own initiate. This street was still being held by the enemy at the time. Since those two streets are parallel and there's an open view from one of these streets to the other, at one point in time we noticed him crossing Sava Kovacevica Street. This was a hair-raising experience for me because I was certain at the time that he would be captured by the enemy and probably killed. I don't know how, but he got lucky and he returned safe and in one piece. I know one thing. From this moment on I banned him from being in any place where his life might have been in danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You heard about the allegations concerning your interview to a journalist Slavoljub Kacarevic. What can you tell us about that interview with journalist Kacarevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't even know his name at the time. This occurred on the 24th of November, the day we returned to Belgrade. It was in the kitchen of Stanko Vujanovic's father's house. The two of us were alone. I don't remember whether his photographer was there, too, but I do believe that we were alone. I know that I was in no mood for interviews. He tried to talk me into it, tried to talk me into feeding him some information. Eventually, I agreed to talk to him. I gave him a rough account of the situation along my axis of operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. During this interview, did he take any notes? Did he take sporadic notes or was he taking notes all the time or was he in fact recording this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he had a notebook on him. I know that occasionally he wrote things down, but he was trying to have a conversation. I wasn't dictating my account to him. We were just talking. There is a situation I would like to tell the Chamber about. In the course of this conversation I told him that along the axis of operations of my company there may have been over a thousand soldiers. His understanding was that I was being boastful, at least that's my take on it, which was absolutely ridiculous. I never told him that I was in command of all those soldiers, but his impression was that I was being boastful and that I was boasting about having commanded over a thousand soldiers. In actual fact, what I was trying to do was put him in the picture. The OTP are saying that I told him certain things; well, I'm giving you my own testimony now. I did talk to that journalist and I tried to explain to him that I had previously trained a unit from Kragujevac the strength of a battalion, comprising perhaps 400 or 500 soldiers. These soldiers now came to our axis of operations, and I had managed to train them to stand guard, to secure the liberated areas. There were between 400 and 500 of those; I didn't exactly keep track. One thing that I can say is that among those and among the other soldiers along my axis and along all the other axes, there were those who described themselves as Chetniks. But a Chetnik unit could never have survived there, nor would I have ever agreed to being command of a self-styled Chetnik unit. I know who the Chetniks were. I was no Chetnik officer; I was a JNA officer. I assume that it was based on that story that Mr. Kacarevic wrote what he wrote. If any further explanations are necessary, I'll be happy to provide those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard the evidence here of a member of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have two problems here. One of them is that we have no notice of this particular incident, but the more important problem is this counsel, this Defence counsel, has never put this matter to Mr. Kacarevic. Mr. Kacarevic came and testified as a journalist and this story that he's coming up with today was never put before him that he's confused as to these 400 to 500 soldiers. In their opening statement this has never been placed into testimony. This is the first time today that we're hearing that this reporter was confused what this person had said, made a mistake on what this person had said. We have never had any notice. They've had the opportunity to put their case to that witness and it was not done; in fact, they brought out the best facts they could from that particular story. As a result, this testimony should not come in because it hasn't been properly put to the witness when they had the opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. It will be a matter we will consider when we come to weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was the OTP, of all people, pushing this piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is the right of every indictee --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we're trying to help you move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I apologise. I jumped the gun on this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday we tendered into evidence the map which you drew and marked your own axes of operations with the four stages. This is exhibit 785. You drew two lines to mark your axes of operations. Can you please try to be a little more specific about this. How broad was the area covered by your operations? Because the way you drew it, it wasn't that easy to understand the breadth of the area covered. As briefly and specifically as you can, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The breadth of a company's operations in a built-up area is defined by the conditions prevailing in this built-up area. Given the peculiarities of fighting in a built-up area, the front is much narrower as a rule in relation to fighting going on out in the open.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There, you have the map in front of you. Can you please try to mark the exact breadth of this area. Is it the way you drew it yesterday or could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right-hand boundary would be Nova Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the left-hand boundary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vergaseva Street and as far as Leva Supoderica Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can be very specific about all the streets that were included in this area if you think that is required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was only interested in the exact boundaries of your operations area. What about the area in which your observation post was positioned, did you have any prisoners there or any detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of combat operations, did you ever have occasion to visit the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the combat operations in Vukovar, did you ever go to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Radomir Dejanovic; and if yes, was he your friend and did he actually study with you at one point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time that I heard of his name was in this courtroom. I had never ever met him or got introduced to him in any way before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of the combat operations in Vukovar, did you at any point personally take the prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica at any point and in any manner whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never ever did I take any prisoners anywhere, and I had never been to Sremska Mitrovica in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: Did you at any point in time and place before and during the Vukovar operations, did you have any agreements with Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and the members of the Territorial Defence, either altogether or individually, regarding the people from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with regard to any issues related to Vukovar, except the commands -- the chain of command with regard to Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I studied in military schools from the secondary military school all the way up to the academy, I learned one thing, and that is that the relationship between the superior and his subordinate is very clearly defined. The superior commander is responsible to maintain this relationship and for the nature of it. There can be no discussions, no agreements. The superior issues orders to the subordinate and is responsible for the actions of his subordinate. So I did not have any discussions or talks, nor did it occur to me -- I did not think that it was possible at all. And in particular, I would not have any discussions, I would not be reaching any agreements or arrangements of the nature that I have been charged with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 10th of November, 1991, did you have command and control or any other kind of effective control of the Territorial Defence troops and the Leva Supoderica unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally take part in the taking out and the selection of 400 non-Serbs from the Vukovar Hospital on the 20th of November, 1991, and did you in any way whatsoever take part in the evacuation of those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't even witness personally the events that you described, let alone participated in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were in the Vukovar area, did you have any knowledge of the crime at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can assert as an officer, as a commanding officer, that I would have taken appropriate measures against any person, even if that person had been my own brother, had I known at all of any crimes. And I can also assert that I did not get any information until 1992, as I have already described in my evidence when I read in the paper, that something had happened at Ovcara. So I had no knowledge up until that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that the non-Serbs captured in Vukovar received any death threats and that the members of the Territorial Defence and the Leva Supoderica Detachment were about to commit any crimes against them, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is something that I have already asked you, but I want you to state this very clearly. Did you have regular meetings in Stanko Vujanovic's father's house with Miroljub Vujovic, Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Stanko Vujanovic, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was a troop officer; I was not a staff officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any point make a selection of the prisoners that were to be put on the buses at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time on the orders of Veselin Sljivancanin or any other person take out 15 prisoners from the bus at the Vukovar barracks and took them back to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I never received any such orders from Mr. Sljivancanin, nor was I ever in a situation to bring anyone back from the barracks to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As for witness P022, did he at any point tell you that he had committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he had told me that, there would have been no need for him to be court-martialed at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did at any point witness P002, did he talk to you on the 21st of November, 1991, about the events at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a fabricated story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know and do you know who (redacted) is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in Vukovar, I had never ever heard of that person, before I arrived in Vukovar and later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see, got introduced, or got to know (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever get introduced to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know who that is, only in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only what I heard in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did (redacted), was he ever on your axis of operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... these names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which ones are they, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So now we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one more question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you heard about the crime at Ovcara. What is your attitude towards this crime today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never in my whole life have I condoned crimes, and not only crimes, but any error that might endanger anyone's life. I'm so sorry that I had never been in a situation to use my knowledge and my will and determination to assist any of those people who had been captured, and I abhor the way in which they were liquidated. And I think that there is no honour, no chivalry, no humanity in those actions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded my examination-in-chief and we are, in fact, getting close to our time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are past our time for the break, Mr. Borovic, and we will need now to have a half-hour break because of the redactions. We will resume at 25 minutes to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have concluded my examination-in-chief of this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood, Mr. Borovic, that you or your client wanted to add something; that's why I called on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much. I would like to ask Mr. Radic, although in fact I was originally thinking of asking this in my re-direct, but now I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your attitude towards the indictment and everything that has been said here, or if you have anything in particular to say to the Chamber at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my English is so bad that the gentleman from the registry probably did not understand what I wanted to say. I merely sought the permission to address you. I wanted to ask you that all the Defence counsel from other Defence teams and the gentlemen from the OTP, they use all the documents, all the arguments at their disposal and -- to ask anything they want to ask because I have been waiting for this moment for the last 11 years. And I want to be able to personally defend my own honour, the honour of my family, and the honour of my profession, and I would not like for anyone observing this trial to criticise me and to say that there was any reason, any fault on my part for -- because of which there -- some things may not have come to light. I have to apologise to my Defence counsel, Mr. Borovic, this is not something that we've discussed. I hope that he won't get angry with me. I'm saying this because you restricted the right of the Prosecution to use some documents, but I would like to ask you to allow them to use any documents that they want to confront me with. So this is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your view of the indictment? And now, as for your desire to be confronted with documents, the Chamber has already ruled on this issue so you will not have this opportunity to see the documents that cannot be admitted. This is not something that we discussed. This is not something for the two of us to discuss. This is a procedural matter. But as far as the indictment is concerned, as far as your voluntary surrender is concerned, this is not something that I asked you about. But since now you are in position to say so, can you now tell us: How did you make this decision and what is your view of the indictment? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take part in any action that I am charged with in the indictment. I never committed any crime. I never issued any order that might result in any crimes. At the beginning of the trial, I pleaded not guilty and this is something that I still maintain. I'm not guilty. But I would once again like to make sure -- I would like to ask you to allow all the parties to ask any questions whatsoever, despite the position taken by my Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when -- when you decided to surrender yourself voluntarily to the Tribunal, how did this come about? What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had thought for many years that I would never come before this Tribunal because I know that there is no reason, no cause for me to be here. But when I realised that this would be inevitable, from that moment on I have felt this need to say things in defence of myself, my family, my honour, my dignity. I feel the need to say things that, in my opinion, need to be said. I personally thought that with the arrival of Mr. Mrksic one year before I came here, it would become clear to everyone that all the allegations in the indictment have nothing whatsoever to do with me. But the situation is as we see it now. I am now here, and I ask everyone to ask me all the questions that they see fit. And, Mr. Borovic, I would like to ask you to make that possible, to allow everyone to ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radic. Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Very well. Mr. Domazet, is there any matter you wish to raise with Mr. Radic on behalf of your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But Mr. Radic -- or rather, Mr. Mrksic's Defence does not have any questions for Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I will have a few questions. I will try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radic, there's no need for me to introduce myself. I will be asking you a few questions related to the claims -- allegations made by the Prosecution in the indictment that are relevant for my Defence and I will also refer to some of the questions asked by my colleague, Mr. Borovic. So please answer very briefly to those few questions that I have for you. Did you personally hear of any agreement -- Mr. Borovic asked you about agreements between Mrksic, my client, and yourself as alleged in the indictment. What I want to ask you is whether you have heard of any agreements that the Croats remaining in the Vukovar Hospital after the fall of Vukovar to be tortured, maltreated and killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear whether there were any ideas to that effect in your circle where you were moving that there were people and that such people should be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified about Mr. Seselj's visit, so I'm going to ask you about certain allegations from the indictment. In that period in Vukovar, did you hear from anyone re-telling alleged -- the alleged sentence by Seselj that no Ustasha can leave Vukovar alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. If I may say so, this is ridiculous. Who is Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you specific questions which relate to the allegations in the indictment. Did you hear from anyone this idea that no Ustasha can leave Vukovar alive? It doesn't have to be connected to Seselj, but it can be something that was said by anyone in your environment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not hear anything like that before I came to this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'm going to ask you something that I'm interested in and maybe you can give me answers relating to some other assertions that you heard during this trial. I heard from your testimony that practically during your combat operations you had contacts with Dusan Jaksic and Miroljub Vujovic. Did you have personal contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did have contacts with Mr. Jaksic, but it was a visual contact only. At the command post of the command of the 1st Motorised Battalion or the 1st Assault Detachment. I didn't have any need to discuss or to talk with him about anything or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Since I'm interested in him primarily, I'm going to put two further questions relating to that gentleman. Did you personally hear anything about the ways and the reasons and who actually replaced him and why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any information about him being replaced. I have no reason to doubt his words either when he says that he was replaced, but I don't have any knowledge about that. I do know that members of the Territorial Defence were not satisfied with his work, and this dissatisfaction of theirs was expressed. And I believe him and I believe the commander of my battalion, Major Tesic, I believe that this was expressed to him and to the commander of my battalion. I think that I was not present at any conversation relating to his replacement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the substance of their dissatisfaction with his work? Do you remember any objections that they made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a staff officer. He never wanted to get his boots dirty, and that was the main reason for the dissatisfaction of the other members of the TO. What I mean is that according to them, he did not have the courage to go to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic asked you yesterday about my client. You explained and you testified that he never issued any orders to you on combat actions or any other types of orders. What I would like to ask you is that whether the senior officers that you did have contact with during combat operations - I am thinking of Zirojevic, the 2nd Company Commander; Bojkovski, the other commanding officers that you had contact with - did you ever hear from them if Sljivancanin ever issued any orders to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Allow me to -- just to say briefly. I personally think that Major Sljivancanin was not familiar with our assignments. And for that reason, and especially because he was the security chief in the Guards Brigade, he could not issue any orders to me, in any case. I did not hear from any other commander of other companies that he issued orders to anyone else either. I believe that many things that I have stated just now are coming as a surprise to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, actually he did tell me during the break that he was surprised with a lot of things that you said in your testimony, but this is not the subject of my questions now. We heard from the testimony of a certain witness that my client was in charge, that he was in command of all the operations, and so on and so forth. And this relates to what we have just said because this is the testimony of a witness who testified on the 10th of April of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, I do not have the specific transcript page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time during combat operations send a report to Sljivancanin about the combat operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When visiting my unit, I was obliged to inform Mr. Sljivancanin with the current situation, to inform him about what I knew in relation to information that he sought. He would usually request to know what was going on with the soldiers, did we have any information about captured soldiers, did we have any captives, did we seize any weapons. This is the information that I would provide to Major Sljivancanin. He was an officer from my superior command. He was an authority figure to me, not just to me, but for all of us commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague, Ms. Tapuskovic is helping me now. The page that I needed -- the page reference is page 7.395. Well, let me put it to you this way: Do you know whether Mr. Sljivancanin's headquarters was near -- was near Vuteks in Radiceva Ulica or do you know where the headquarters were? I'm not going to use that word "headquarters," but do you know where the premises of the security section were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the words by a witness. I remember that Mr. Sljivancanin, as part of the staff of the motorised brigade command was located in the village of Negoslavci. I was in that house on the 13th and the 14th. At one time, once on the 13th, once on the 14th of November, when I sought the approval from a clerk, a desk officer, Zoran Momcilovic to go to Belgrade. That is the only time when I went to that facility in Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were going to Belgrade. Was that the regular procedure for a commanding officer to leave? Why were you asking for this permission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to be able to pass through all the check-points to enter Belgrade and to return from Belgrade, I had to have a pass for my vehicle. The pass had to be in my name and would make it possible for me to go and to return. I received this permission on the 13th, and on the 14th I dropped by at the command post in order to tell the gentleman, Zoran Momcilovic that I was actually at that point in time leaving for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One last question relating to the statement of a witness, you will probably recall which witness it was. Did you hear that Major Sljivancanin ever went around Vukovar in an armoured vehicle and with a loudspeaker was heard to say that Vukovar was liberated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear of that and I didn't see it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My name is Phil Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor and I'm going to be asking you some questions. Now, during the war in Vukovar, you fought with soldiers from the Vukovar TO. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As well as volunteers and members of the Leva Supoderica unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the remark that volunteers did not have a separate unit; they were part of the TO forces. They were used to replenish the ranks of the TO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's correct. And you fought with them along your -- that axis, that same axis, for several weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And this was urban fighting or urban street fighting where you fought house-to-house, street-to-street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We fought, on the one hand, against the Croatian forces, which happened to be on the other side in conditions that you have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the fighting was fierce, wasn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Any fighting is fierce.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, this was guerilla-style fighting, if you want to call it, as opposed to two large armies approaching each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will correct you. It was combat in a populated place where there were two armed formations and the fighting in an inhabited location is one of the most difficult forms of combat between two opposing sides. I cannot define whether it's -- the proper term for it is guerilla fighting or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And it's a very difficult form of fighting, and members of the TO and volunteers as well as JNA were killed. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During fighting, during assault operations, there were casualties on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the question was: Members of the TO, volunteers, and JNA were killed. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were killed in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. And others were injured and maimed. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And people were -- and soldiers were psychologically affected. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to describe the category -- the term you name soldiers in the following way. There were soldiers on the side I was on who were in a special psychological state. I'm referring to soldiers who arrived with me together from Belgrade who were members of the 3rd Motorised Company. A large number of the TO members and volunteers already had certain combat experience, and I did not form the impression that they were under any kind of psychological pressure. They, I would say, withstood these conditions of heavy fighting much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you referred, meaning the members of the JNA, your commanders, as well as members of the TO, and volunteers referred to the enemy you were fighting as "Ustasha." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot recall using that term, but I can say with a lot of responsibility that at the time that term was used because the circumstances we were in at the time for the opposing side for soldiers, which we at the time considered to be paramilitary soldiers of the Croatian side, were called Ustashas. We called them Ustashas. That does not mean that all Croats were Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And members of the TO, volunteers, and Leva Supoderica were hostile to the enemy or the Ustasha soldiers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all hostile to the enemy. What else were we supposed to be if they were on one side and we were on the other? The enemy side was also hostile to us in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And as TO members, Leva Supoderica members, volunteers were killed, hostility increased, whether they were killed or whether people were injured, hostility would increase. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. You are using terms TO members, Leva Supoderica members, and volunteers. I assert here that all volunteers were within the TO ranks or Leva Supoderica ranks, meaning that the volunteer formation -- there was no volunteer formation on the axis where I was. As to whether hostilities grew, I didn't notice that. There was hostility from the first to the last moment, but I couldn't tell to what extent and to what -- or what its intensity was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about that middle period and then we'll get back to the hostility. From November 10th onward, you knew that the JNA troops would succeed in Vukovar. You'd taken Milovo hill and you were moving towards the Danube. You knew you'd succeed from the middle part of November onward. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Look, I'm a soldier. When I'm given an assignment, I want to carry that assignment out --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will use --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- the question is: From the middle part of November onward, you knew that you would succeed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was what we aspired to, to be successful. I wasn't looking into the future as to when that would happen, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And liberation or so-called liberation occurred on November 18th, a little over a week later. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And having fought closely with the Leva Supoderica - or if you want to call them all TO people, TO soldiers - did you anticipate any acts of retaliation or revenge at that time, knowing the hostility that was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my communication with the Leva Supoderica Detachment or the TO was cut off, not because I wanted it to but by an order of my commander of the 10th of October -- 10th of November, excuse me. From that point on, I had no need to know what Leva Supoderica was doing or what the TO members were doing from that point on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir, that's not the question. The question is: Having fought closely with those people and being aware of the hostility, did you anticipate any acts of retaliation or revenge? That's the question, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am answering your questions like this: I cooperated with them until the 10th of November. After that, and even before that, I had no need --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that's the question. The question is: Did you anticipate from that unit or the TO any acts of revenge? That's the question. You can answer yes, you can answer no, you can answer maybe. Did you anticipate any acts of revenge or retaliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't anticipate anything. I didn't have any need to anticipate anything at that point in time, not from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, we've had testimony here from witness Van Lynden, a reporter, who testified that he was fearful of a massacre occurring between the soldiers and Chetniks who were drunk and firing weapons. He and the other reporters were worried - and that's at pages 3118 and 3119 - but you didn't anticipate any retaliation, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is an objection in principle. I'm not going to protect Radic and intervene when I think that there are other irregular questions. But I think it was so far the position of the Court that when a statement by a witness is mentioned, the name of the witness should not be mentioned and the contents of the statement are mentioned in a slightly different way. But I think -- maybe there's no need to go into that so much now, but I think that there should be on the part of the Prosecutor an awareness that the question needs to be put differently.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was something that Mr. Van Lynden saw. I did not see a single Chetnik unit with my own eyes. I'm not saying that certain members of the forces who were on the side of the Yugoslav People's Army did not feel themselves to be members of the Chetniks, that they did not declare themselves as Chetniks. But I did not see a formation calling itself a Chetnik formation ever in my life, meaning --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, there is a mistake in the transcript. It says "members of the JNA" feeling or considering themselves as Chetniks. That is something the witness did not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, we've had as an exhibit in this case, Exhibit 415, 415, which is an order from General Panic. And General Panic indicates that he is concerned of retaliation or revenge by the Territorial Defence. Now, sir, that was on the 18th of November, 1991. You still didn't anticipate any acts of revenge or retaliation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the command and control system, the chief of the General Staff can address his inferior or subordinate officers in writing. I assume that this was the command of the 1st Military District. That order, then, also in writing, is relayed by the commander of the 1st Army District to the commander of the operations group, that was Colonel Mrksic. Colonel Mrksic, either by a written or oral order, can issue the battalion commanders or the assault group commanders assignments arising from that order, while the battalion commander decides what he would say or what he would order his subordinate commanders and companies to do. So if on that day I was the commander, the komandir, of the 3rd Company, all the orders that the battalion commander, Major Tesic, issued to me or his deputy issued to me, I - I assert here - carried them out. On the 18th of November, I did not have any contact with the Territorial Defence or the Leva Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you receive notice from your superior, Major Tesic, to be worried or to be concerned about acts of retaliation and revenge by TO members or soldiers on November 18th and 19th? Did you receive that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that Major Tesic said anything to us, the company commanders, about the activities, possible assignments relating to the Territorial Defence. There was no need for that at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Major Trifunovic has testified that it was reasonable to assume that acts of retaliation could occur, but do you still want to maintain that you did not anticipate any acts of revenge? Is that what you'd like to maintain, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, Major Trifunovic is an officer from the superior command. He was a staff officer. I never saw Major Trifunovic at the front line where the fighting was going on. As for what he may have meant and for what he may have stated, well that's his own position and there's nothing I can say about it. What I can tell you is that I never knew or heard from any of my superior officers about any warnings in relation to the TO or the Leva Supoderica unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you, sir, did not warn Major Tesic and say to him: Having fought with some of these people who were not professional soldiers and knowing their hostility, you better be very careful about acts of retaliation and revenge? You never said that, did you, sir, to your commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, in everyday communication with Major Tesic, at least three or four times during a single day I found myself talking to him in terms of informing him about what was going on so that as a result at every single point in time he was always fully aware of anything going on in my unit. There was really no special exceptional need for me to brief him on anything at all, such as you have just defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So I take it that the answer is no, sir. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for your allegations, they are not true. The hostility that you mention was something that went without saying. We were fighting paramilitary units. You can't expect that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir, the question is: Did you warn Major Tesic that there were volunteers and unprofessional soldiers in the TO and Leva Supoderica who were hostile and could take acts of revenge and retaliation? I believe your answer is no. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why would I do anything like that? I never knew they were planning any sort of revenge or retaliation to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you had been in -- a member of the Guards Motorised Brigade for some time. And in 1991, were there any other Captain Radics within the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're not aware of any other Captain Radics in Vukovar in October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So when Dr. Njavro stated or testified that a captain introduced himself on November 19th as Captain Radic, you're not aware of any other Captain Radic being at the hospital on November 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a fabrication by Mr. Njavro.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When witness P30 states that Captain Radic was outside the Vukovar Hospital receiving orders from Major Sljivancanin on November 20th, you're not aware of any other Captain Radic being in Vukovar on that date, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I've answered that. I have no knowledge of there being yet another Captain Radic in the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you did go to the hospital on the 19th. Isn't that correct, sir? You testified to that yesterday at pages 60 and 61?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you were also at the Vukovar Hospital on November 18th, on the previous day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.
