utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Njavro has testified that you were at the hospital on both the 18th and 19th. Isn't it a fact that you went to the hospital on both the 18th and 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade, of which I was a member, entered the hospital in the manner that I described on the 19th, not on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've given two statements in Belgrade. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I provided one statement to the security administration officers, and the other statement I provided was before the military court in Belgrade back in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you tell the truth when you gave those statements? Were you truthful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was truthful, and I was saying things based on my memory, everything that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you would agree that in 1998 you had a better memory about these incidents because it was much closer in time to now, which is almost ten years later than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the first statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's 03054580 through 4582 in English and in the B/C/S it's 02188354 to 8357 in the B/C/S. Could we please go to page 1 in the B/C/S 02188354, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look below the word "statement," do you see in the middle, sir, where it says: "In the afternoon hours of 18 November"? Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read that. "In the afternoon hours of 18 November 1991, at the orders of battalion commander Major Borivoj Tesic, I set off from the worker's club with a group of soldiers and headed towards Vukovar Hospital, crossing territory which units had not searched and reached the hospital grounds at around 1500 hours on 18 November 1991 from the direction of the town centre over the middle bridge." Is that what that says there? Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know you signed that statement on the following page -- on page 3 of that statement -- I'm sorry, page 4. Your statement is on that statement. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you gave a second statement to the military court on December 17th, 1998. Do you recall that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And before giving that statement, you were warned that you were to tell the truth and not to hold anything back. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were also given a perjury warning. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were warned that perjury is a crime. Do you recall being warned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. We could look at that. Could we go to -- in the English it's 0303-2056 to 2058. And in the B/C/S it's 02188288 to 8290. Sir, if you go to page number 2, first, which is 02188288. And just very briefly, do you see the warning, the words "perjury" there by 231, in relation to Article 231? Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now -- so you were warned to tell the truth and you were warned about perjury. Now, let's go to page 2 in the English which is page 3 in the B/C/S which is page 02188289 in the B/C/S to the second full paragraph which begins with: "Only on 18, November 1991." Do you see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll read that. "Only on 18 November 1991 did I receive a task from battalion commander Major Borivoj Tesic to organise with my unit the securing of the Vukovar Hospital grounds and not to allow unauthorised persons to enter or leave the Vukovar Hospital grounds. I performed this task for less than 24 hours, because on the next day, on 19 November 1991, I transferred securing of the Vukovar Hospital grounds to a military police unit." Did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if you continue on to the end of this document, you state -- go to the next page. "I read the record and it contains everything I said, and I hereby sign it without any remarks." And you signed that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Having given two statements in 1998, which you signed, stating that you went to the hospital on November 18th, will you now agree that the first time you went to that hospital, the Vukovar Hospital, was on November 18th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you're changing your testimony since Dr. Njavro has placed you at that hospital on November 18th abusing patients? Isn't that why you're changing your statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Do you want me to explain this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back in 1993, I quit my career as a professional soldier in the JNA. Between 1993 and early 1998, my new job was something that had nothing to do with the JNA at all. Throughout this time I was not at all in touch, nor did I meet anyone at all from the Guards Brigade, no one at all that I could talk to and evoke what had occurred in Vukovar. I don't remember the specific date, but I think it was wintertime early 1998. One morning I got a phone call from one of my former professors who taught me the subject that we call security back at the academy. He called me at home and told me that I was to go to the security administration, so that we could discuss something. He also asked me to come right away. Given the fact that this was the first such call ever in my life, many years after the termination of my active-duty service, I packed my things immediately and I was off to the security administration headquarters, which at the time was in the General Staff building. On arriving there, I was met by a colonel whose last name I believe to have been Bjelinac, Bjelinac. And there were two other persons sitting there, one in uniform and one in plain clothes. He told me that they wanted to speak to me about the time in Vukovar and about my memory of my time in Vukovar. I was a professional soldier back then, and I knew what sort of an institution the security administration was. So I accepted to talk to these people. This man named Bjelinac left and the man who stayed with me was a colonel who I later learned was called Tomic. I don't remember the name of the other one. They interviewed me about everything that I remembered in relation to Vukovar. After the interview they told me that they would draw up an official note and that there should be a typist present who would take this down. I had no problem with that at all. A lady came over with a typewriter. We reconstructed my entire account. Mr. Tomic dictated my statement to her and all the allegations I made. I was there for any corrections that I deemed necessary. What I'm trying to point out is, that day I was entirely unprepared and it was all out of the blue that I was dragged there to be interviewed by these people about things that I had not been thinking about for the previous five or six years. My memory at the time suggested that I did go to the hospital on the 19th of November. Why did I draw that inference at the time is really not something that I can explain now. What I can say with sure and certain knowledge is that I never entered the hospital at my own initiative, I never set foot there, I never lingered in the hospital, and I never ever mistreated anybody at all, let alone a wounded person --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I provided that statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I provided that statement, I did not wish to deviate from my account before the military court. I was fully conscious of the fact that I had done nothing of which I should be ashamed. I repeated my account before the military court with no intention of hiding anything, altering anything, sweeping anything under the carpet to prevent anything from becoming generally known. My conviction at the time is that this had occurred on the 18th, not because I was trying to conceal something. However, when I arrived here, when I started delving into this case, when I realised that this case was nothing but a continuation of my own life, when I received all the documents which I then first laid eyes on, when I started remembering all the details, when I started thinking through this as hard as I could, I started remembering exactly what had occurred on the 18th and the 19th, those two crucial days. I kept thinking about those days, and I can now assert before this honourable Trial Chamber with full responsibility that I never did anything to put anyone's life at risk, not my own side, not the enemy, nor would there ever have been a motive for me to try and do anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you have no writings or no diary indicating the dates that you went to the hospital. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Much as all other active-duty officers, officers and NCOs, I did keep what we call a working notebook. However, when I quit active service I handed over all my documents, as we are supposed to under the law, so that no document was left in my own private archive. I don't have any documents left from the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you have no writings, sir. And having no writings, the earliest writings that we have in this court, sir, are those in which you say you went to the hospital on November 18th. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll try to explain how exactly this was. I'm not saying anything. I do believe that I made a factual error at the time when I specified this date. There is no escaping from that. I have been given an opportunity to explain, and I wish to continue my involvement in this discussion regarding the specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, continue on that, sir. You just testified a few minutes ago that you would never go to the hospital on your own initiative, and that's -- that's about page 55, I believe, 54, 55. On page 54 you never "entered the hospital at my own initiative." Sir, would it surprise you that Major Tesic has told an investigative judge that he never gave you orders to secure the hospital and that you did this against his specific orders? Does that surprise you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that does surprise me and how. I don't know what Mr. Tesic's reasons are or what he remembers; however, the moment he ordered me to go to the hospital and secure the building with my soldiers until the military police arrived, we were not there alone. There were many officers surrounding us. On the other hand, I am convinced, since I read Major Tesic's statement, that it wasn't Captain Bojkovski who had received that assignment and it wasn't he and his soldiers securing the hospital, as Mr. Tesic had originally stated. I am telling you that it wasn't Captain Zirojevic either. I'm telling you that there was no other unit carrying out that task, and I'm also telling you that Major Tesic would not have been able to accomplish this task with the soldiers at his command alone. I am telling you that I secured the hospital building until the arrival of the military police. My unit was then withdrawn from this assignment, and we took no further steps within the hospital compound or in the hospital building itself, not myself, not my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you agree, sir, that Major Tesic says he doesn't know why you were at the hospital because he never ordered you there, that you had no right to be there? Are you saying Major Tesic is wrong, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you purposely went to the hospital in violation of Major Tesic's orders to determine who was impersonating the medical staff and the wounded? Isn't that why you were at that hospital, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I appreciate your efforts. I understand everything you're trying to put to me. However, what you have just suggested is something that no officer would ever do. I would have been supposed to go a kilometre deep into an area that I had never previously been to only to establish what was going on at the hospital? Why would I have wanted to know? What would have been my objective? What would have been my reason for going there? I couldn't give a hoot about what was going on at the hospital. I can assert with full responsibility, had Major Tesic never ordered me to go there, I would never have set foot in that hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You didn't care what was going on in the hospital, but you just wound up there again on the 20th of November to see what was happening there. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not certain of the times. Do we brake at 12.45 today or 1.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We do specifically, Mr. Weiner, if that's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at 2.00. We finish this evening at 5.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday -- we're staying with the hospital. Yesterday you testified that you followed Major Tesic in to the hospital, and you eventually realised that Sergeant Jovic and two other JNA injured were there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I explained how I came to be in the hospital, and I explained that for a very brief time -- in fact, briefly after Major Tesic entered the hospital I did the same, and this is where I saw Sergeant Jovic and two other JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you didn't go in there intentionally to see Sergeant Jovic and the JNA wounded, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I followed the battalion commander in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So it wasn't your intention to see those people in the hospital, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that Sergeant Jovic was in the hospital itself, and I was not surprised when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But when you went into the hospital, it wasn't your intention to see Sergeant Jovic and the other two injured JNA soldiers, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot now say to you what my intention was at the time. The fact is that I went into the hospital itself immediately after my battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you testified that you spoke with Sergeant Jovic but you didn't take him out of there or escort him out. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him. We exchanged a couple of sentences. It was a very brief encounter, and it is true that I did not take him out of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could we look again at your second statement which is 03032056 to 2057, page 2 in the English. In the B/C/S it's 02188287 to 02188290 on page 8289, please. And could you go to 8289, please. There you go. Now, if you look at the third -- the second full paragraph which is -- appears to be the third paragraph which begins with: "On 18 November 1991 ..." If you go down to the bottom of that paragraph you state - and you're referring to securing the Vukovar Hospital on the 18th - you say: "While we were securing Vukovar Hospital, I entered it only once with battalion commander Major Borivoj Tesic, accompanied by soldiers who were my personal escort to take out three JNA Yugoslavian People's Army soldiers who had been taken prisoner" --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text does not say the 18th of November but the 19th of November. You just said the 18th, so could this please be corrected, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If you read the full paragraph it's clear because he said he transferred on the following day and then he says while securing, so it's a reference to the 18th. I'll be happy to read the full paragraph to make you happy. "Only on 18 November 1991 did I receive a task from battalion commander Major Borivoj Tesic to organise with my unit the securing of Vukovar Hospital grounds and not to allow unauthorised persons to enter or leave the Vukovar Hospital grounds. I performed this task for less than 24 hours because on the next day, on 19 November, I transferred securing of Vukovar Hospital grounds to a military police unit commanded by Milovo Simic. While we were securing the hospital, I entered it only once with battalion commander Major Borivoj Tesic, accompanied by soldiers who were my personal escort, to take out three JNA (Yugoslav People's Army) who had been taken prisoners and two nurses. After taking these prisoners and two nurses, I did not enter the premises of the Vukovar Hospital nor did I have any need to do so." Now, sir -- first, did I read that correctly, sir? Is that what it states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And was your purpose of entering to take those JNA soldiers out or did you just come upon them like you stated yesterday while following Major Tesic into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of my visit to the hospital was to secure the hospital until the arrival of the military police on the orders of the commander, Borivoj Tesic. And the activities that followed after we actually entered the hospital itself, I did not have any control over them; and since my commander was present there, he was in control. When I said to take out three soldiers and two nurses, I meant us, those of us who were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, however, you testified that you didn't escort those persons out. In 1998 you said you did escort those persons out. Which is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take them out personally, nor was I present in the hospital at the time when they left; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You didn't take them out personally but you wrote or you stated: "After taking out these prisoners and the two nurses, I did not enter the premises of Vukovar Hospital." So if you didn't take them out, why did you previously state you did take them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I gave this statement before a military court, as far as I can remember in the course of my testimony before the military court, when I was called as a witness in a trial against unknown persons who had committed the crime at Ovcara, I replied to the questions that were asked by the presiding judge. And after I actually replied, the judge dictated for the record a version of my reply. At that time I did not think that he had made any mistakes because in terms of a description of the event, it corresponded to the actual situation. So I apologise, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was inside only once, in the hospital itself I mean. The image that I have is very dark. A large number of people being there in conditions that were not appropriate for a hospital, so it was a gloomy picture. I did see Sergeant Jovic there and two reserve soldiers. I was there with Major Tesic and some other JNA troops. Captain Sasa Bojkovski was in there, too, and some other soldiers, a couple of other soldiers. At that time I felt uncomfortable, and I did not want to stay there. And there was absolutely no need for me to linger there for a single moment. The moment I left that part of the hospital, I never returned, never. I have never in my whole life revisited that part of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you indicated that the -- you gave a statement to the investigative judge and that he got it wrong. However, on the last page, sir, of this statement you indicated: "I have nothing else to add. I dictated my statement and read it. It contains everything I said, and I hereby sign it without any remarks." You then sign that as your statement. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1998 I found myself for the first time in my life before a Trial Chamber. Up until that time, I had not had an opportunity to even see how it -- what it looks like. I never committed any kinds of infractions to traffic violation that would bring me in front of a Trial Chamber. At that time, I did not feel that it was so important for every single letter to be put down the way I think it should be. So it is stated here that I was in the hospital. I was in the hospital. The statement says that three soldiers, Sergeant Jovic and two soldiers, were taken out. They were taken out, but I did not know that it should be so specific and so precise. So I'm now telling you that I did not order them to go out because I did not have the authority to do so; it was Major Tesic who ordered that. And I am stating here and now that I did not take part in the taking out of the -- of Sergeant Jovic and the two soldiers because nobody had asked me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So your earlier statement is wrong again, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to apologise. My statement is not wrong. I just think that it's imprecise. I am sure that I would have been as precise in my statement at that time had I paid more attention to that. At that time I thought that it did not contain any false statements. It is just that I saw it in the way that I just explained to you. I am very unhappy that the statement is imprecise, but there was no ill intention behind it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. While you're in the hospital you walked past offices and rooms and you see people inside the hospital, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered the hospital, I remember that it was a small room located in the hall to the left. So at that time I did not notice other offices, but I saw people observing us. They were in a very difficult situation, at least to my mind. And this impression was very uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, you saw people from several rooms and you saw people who you believed were being disguised as staff or were impersonating staff in white coats. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did notice a certain number of people wearing new coats, and it was obvious that they had been taken for use a moment ago because you could see the creases --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you thought that these people were Croatian paramilitaries, didn't you? That's what your suspicion was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my evidence I stated that I had seen some clothes that had been discarded on the grounds. And, yes, you're right, I believed these people to be Croatian paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And wouldn't it be logical if you think that there are paramilitaries impersonating staff to bring in local people or soldiers that are familiar with the hospital to assess the situation. Isn't that logical, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I was an officer at the time. I was a captain. I was a company commander. I carried out the orders I received from my superiors. What you believe to have been logical at the time is not the same as I do. I was not an adventurer. I did not feel any need for that. I was in the presence of my commander. If he had thought that something needed to be done at any point and in any way, he had the duty and the right to issue an appropriate order to me. I did not take any unauthorised action, and I did not call anyone to do any checks the way that you just suggested to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the first question is a general question. Would it be logical, not for you, but would it be logical, in general, to bring in someone who was local, who had maybe worked at the hospital, who was familiar with the hospital to assess the situation and determine who was disguised -- who, if anyone, was being disguised as hospital staff or patients? Isn't that logical?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you be more specific. Who should think that this was logical?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The JNA, whether it's the military police or the security organ. Would that be logical to do, to bring in someone to check?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to repeat. I was a company commander. My commander was present there. If he felt that some action should be taken along the lines that you just suggested, he would have issued appropriate orders to someone, informed his superior, and now it would be up to them to decide what to do. I was not thinking along those lines, as you just put it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't it the reason that Bogdan Kuzmic was brought to that hospital was for him to assess who was a member of the staff and who wasn't? Wasn't that the reason that Mr. Kuzmic was brought there?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've tried hard to restrain myself, but this is a provocation that -- this is really -- he is really out of line. But so many questions have been asked, and the only question that should have been asked is whether this was indeed within his sphere of authority, security issues and so on. We heard what Mr. Radic said with regard to Mr. Kuzmic. He did not know who Kuzmic was, he didn't know about Bogdan Kuzmic at all, and I would like this question to be rephrased and speculations or other -- in other words, asking the witness to speculate on security issues, I think this goes beyond what this witness can reasonably be expected to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There has been testimony in relation to this defendant and Bogdan Kuzmic on the 18th going from room to room through the hospital, making that determination as to who was in fact a patient, who was in fact staff, and who was not. And that's what I want to raise next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, this is cross-examination. The Prosecution is entitled to put its view to your client and to receive your client's reactions to its view. Its view, obviously, differs from your client's evidence on a number of matters. They are not limited to what your client says occurred in what they can put in cross-examination. So as long as the question is clear, it's, I think, very obvious that your client can say: Well, I know nothing about Kuzmic or whatever it is that he wants to say about it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But if you will allow me. If he wants to confront the witness with what Kuzmic was doing, going from room to room, then he should be very clear about it. And to tell the witness -- to tell Radic: Kuzmic had been going from room to room so that Mr. Radic can then make his mind up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will be observant, Mr. Borovic, if a question is not clear, but I don't see that position at the moment. So carry on, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you and Bogdan Kuzmic went from room to room inspecting patients and staff in that hospital to determine who was impersonating patients and staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true. I would like to say that the first I heard about the man that I had seen accompanying Major Tesic, who had come in with Major Tesic, was when I came here in The Hague. This is the first time that I heard that this person's name was Bogdan Kuzmic. I have never met him, talked to him, or indeed known who he is. So I can assert quite categorically that up to the moment when I entered the hospital, I had not known Bogdan Kuzmic, let alone to accompany him in the hospital and go checking anything in the hospital. So this statement is just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, didn't you look into every room in which it was possible to put hospital personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am an emotional man, and the suffering that I witnessed in this corridor caused me very, very difficult emotions inside me. It never occurred to me to go from room to room and to check who is in there and what is in there. I knew that there are wounded people, sick people there, but it never occurred to me to go checking. And I had no reason to do so, in particular, not with a person that I had never seen in my life up until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at that first statement again, 0305-4580 to 4582, page 2 in the English; 02188355 -- I'm sorry, 8354 at page 8355 in the B/C/S. In the second large paragraph in the B/C/S where you talk about in the presence of Major Tesic at the very entrance to the hospital building and let us continue. "I saw hospital staff in every room in which it was possible to put personnel." Isn't that what it says? "I saw hospital staff --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see what you just read. What this means is -- I think that, again, this is imprecise. What I'm telling you is that I gave this statement to security officers. There is a certain degree of imprecision, but I can assert now that I never went into any rooms, apart from the room where Sergeant Jovic was and the corridor where I went in. I saw the wounded. I saw the sick people. I saw people observing me. I did not feel comfortable at the time, and it was never my intention to do anything else. And I don't think that my commander would have allowed me to do anything in his presence. So I can say that I never walked around the hospital. I went only into that room that was to the left where Sergeant Jovic was, and I remember that there was a bed on wheels, a green one. It was just sitting there. And after that I simply left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Dr. Njavro has testified that he received complaints that you and Mr. Kuzmic went through that hospital room for room on November 18th, inspected patients and personnel, and abused them. Do you deny this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I absolutely deny it for reasons I have already stated. I never met Bogdan Kuzmic in my life. Nobody said to me this is Bogdan Kuzmic and this is Miroslav Radic. We were never introduced. I did not have any reason or need to do anything with Bogdan Kuzmic. I learned the name of that person once I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's continue on at the hospital. You testified that on the 19th of November you left the hospital in Lieutenant Hadzic's care to wait for the arrival of the military police, for them to take over security. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you please show me where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: One moment. Yesterday's testimony on page 66. "I had already left the hospital compound before he returned," and you're referring to Major Tesic, "leaving Second Lieutenant Hadzic to await for the arrival of my military police commanded -- of a military police unit commanded by captain," and it's a mark, it's "Simic." So your testimony is you left the hospitals during the afternoon of November 19th and you left it in the care and custody of Lieutenant Hadzic, and he was the one who waited for the military police and to transfer the custody of -- the control of the hospital compound over to the military police. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us commanders, either of the companies or platoons, were working or carrying out the assignments of our superiors. When you say that I left control to the military police, that implies that the military police company came in accordance with orders of their superior commander, and that on the basis of that order there was a handover of the facility that was being secured, meaning that Lieutenant Hadzic handed over the security duties and Captain Hadzic assumed the security duties for the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you were at the hospital waiting for Captain Simic from the military police, you handed over the custody of that hospital, and then you left with your company? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From what I recall, I was not there during the actual handover of duties. I probably left the hospital compound before that. I don't recall the moment of being face-to-face with Captain Simic and being present at the handover together with him. But I do recall that Lieutenant Hadzic came with soldiers from the hospital to the sector where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you again look to your first 1998 statement, 0305-4580 to 4582. In the B/C/S 02188354 to 02188357 at page 2 which is 8355, please. In the English, page 1 and page 2, the bottom of page 1 and the middle of page 2. 02188354 but at page 8355. I think there is an 8286 there. Now, sir, if you could look at the top paragraph there beginning with "I carried out this task and secured the hospital until 19 November ..." Do you see that? It's the -- begins in the fourth line down. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "I carried out this task and secured the hospital until 19 November 1991, when in the afternoon hours I transferred the security duty to a military police company, that is to its commander, Captain Milivoj Simic. After transferring my duty, I was ordered to assemble the soldiers in my company and carry out a search of the terrain on my direction of operations and collect parts of weapons and equipment." And then if you go down to the fourth paragraph, it's a short paragraph, one up from the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Weiner, with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: There's one other little paragraph and it's on the same issue. "After transferring the duty --" do you see that, sir? It's the fourth paragraph down in the English. It's also the fourth paragraph down in the B/C/S. "After transferring the duty of securing the hospital and its grounds, I withdrew my unit to our previous location, battalion command post sector, where I issued orders to my subordinates about further activities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you just pause there, Mr. Radic. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor read everything correctly except that it was on the 19th in the afternoon, because here in the original text it says "in the morning." This can be very important. That was my intervention; everything else is quite correct. So it's in the morning hours of the 19th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Now, Mr. Radic, can you remember the question and answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Then, now, and always I would say that pertaining to the assignment being carried out by my unit, that is also my personal assignment, which means that if I were to say that I relieved someone, I am responsible for this relief and I would always say that I did it. I am responsible for that. Whether it was done by my company commander in my name, I absolutely accept that as if I were the one who did that. So when it says here in the text "following the handover of the security of the hospital compound I withdrew my unit to the previous location", it means that that was my assignment and I was obliged to implement it. In the course of the implementation, if I transferred my powers to one of the platoon commanders or the squad commanders or anyone else, they had to do it the way the orders instructed them to do it. So I don't believe that in this part of the statement I said anything by mistake or anything wrong. I don't know if you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I understand. But you never said that you transferred the authority to Lieutenant Hadzic and that Lieutenant Hadzic was the one who turned over the control. Isn't that correct? It's not stated here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am trying to tell you this. I, as a company commander, order Lieutenant Hadzic as the platoon commander. And if --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I understand that. But I'm saying, sir, you just didn't say it in this document here. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's move on to the 20th. You've indicated you went to the hospital on the morning of the 20th; that's what you've testified to. Dr. Njavro has testified that you entered the hospital on the morning of the 20th. Are you denying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would just kindly ask you to indicate where I said "morning" is a broad term. Now I'm being asked to be quite specific and precise, so could you please tell me when it was that I said that I left to go to the hospital early in the morning. This is what I understand is being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Page 70 of yesterday's transcript you said that. Now, did you not go in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Look, I went to the hospital at some point. It was probably closer to noon than morning when I went. I categorically state that in the morning hours I was not -- all my recollection indicates that I saw women and men entering buses. I didn't see any action that took place before that, meaning that I wasn't at the hospital at no point in time. I have heard here quite clearly that there was some selection going on, which I did not see myself, that people were being boarded into ambulances. This is something that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that shortly, sir. But Dr. Njavro says that you entered the hospital building on November 20th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness 18 testified that he went with you to the hospital on the 20th, that you entered it, and you met with Major Sljivancanin; and that you, Major Sljivancanin, and Stanko were speaking, and Stanko who was saying who of the injured there, which ones were Ustashas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for witness P18, I state in most responsible terms that that young man at that time, as far as he was concerned, my only objective was not to have him step on some mine, personnel mine or something. This is just an ill-intentioned claim. It's lucky that I managed to save the life -- his life and the lives of others. I most responsibly state that that soldier never, that I'm aware of, came to me. And this story that he told isn't even close to the truth. I don't know what his motives were for telling it, but what he said is absolutely inconceivable to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Witness number 30, who has no apparent relationship to either -- with Dr. Njavro or witness 18. He says that you were out in front of the hospital receiving orders from Major Sljivancanin on the morning of November 20th. Do you know deny that, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I deny it because the way witness P30 explained it, and in view of the fact that I knew who Major Sljivancanin was and that he knew who I was, according to the rules of service, it is regulated how a senior officer or a superior officer addresses a subordinate or junior officer. So it's clear to me, whoever you ask in this courtroom and who did serve in the army, that a senior officer or a superior officer would never address a junior officer in that way. On the other hand, I was not in front of the unit, the line, in the way that P30 explained. I did not command the soldiers of the military police, and I didn't even know that such an activity was underway in the hospital compound. I really don't know what his motives were to say something like that, but I firmly stand on my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So it's your position that these people are all wrong and that you never saw anyone boarding those buses or being placed on those buses on the morning of November 20th or during November 20th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I state responsibly that I never saw any selection. I didn't know that this selection would take place, nobody informed me about it. I didn't see what was being done with those prisoners. The first specific information I had was when I received documents here confirming that. I began to put the pieces together about all the events only when I received the voluminous documents here at The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, weren't you present -- you just said about -- on page -- at about 72 that you were not present when the people got on the ambulances. Weren't you present when the people from the hospital were placed on the buses or were boarding buses? Weren't you present for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I remember is that civilians who were in the hospital compound, they were told that they can choose if they wanted to go to Serbia or to Croatia. So absolutely at no point in time do I recall attending at the hospital when men who had been selected were boarding the buses. So I assert that I did not see any man or any group of men who had been selected in that way to board the buses. I assert that I saw civilians who were allowed to either go to Croatia or to Serbia, and this was only in a very brief time-period. I don't know if they went or where they went; that's something that I don't know, other than what I heard in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody being placed on a bus or anyone boarding buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there was no mention of any coercion or force. People, from what I understood, were going of their own free will. I didn't even see them boarding. All I recall is the detail when they were leaving, going towards the main exit of the hospital compound. I don't know who went where. At the beginning I saw perhaps a couple of buses. As for how long the column was, I never went in that direction and I didn't see that at all. So absolutely there was no coercion there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at your first statement 03054580 through 4582, and in the B/C/S 02188354, page 2 at the bottom going into page 3 on -- which is 8355 in the B/C/S, 02188355. In the English it's on page 2, the fourth full paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is that page 8355? Can you move it down to the -- the last paragraph? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you follow along with me as I read? "As far as the organisation and evacuation of the hospital, I was not a direct participant either in decision-making or its execution, but I was at the hospital grounds at certain times as were other officers of the Guards Brigade. About the evacuation of the hospital, all I can say is that I saw people boarding army buses, and I heard they were being taken in groups to destinations of their choice, either Croatian territory, Vinkovci, Osijek, the Velepromet enterprise grounds in Vukovar, or the army barracks in Vukovar. I did not see anyone being maltreated because there were journalists in the hospital grounds at the time, and they would have certainly registered anything of the kind were it happening. As far as I saw, the evacuation was organised with a military police escort. I do not know who was in charge of evacuating Vukovar Hospital, nor do I know how many people were inside." Sir, you saw people -- first, did I read that correctly? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I was able to just follow the previous page that you read. But I'm sure that you read it all correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Would you like to look at it again or -- or see a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no need. No need. Go ahead. You can put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps he can refer to the statements. He has both statements. I can let him have both statements. He can refer to them, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He doesn't have to, but he should have them at hand in case he wishes to consult them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, so you actually saw the people boarding those buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, in 1998 when I was called to the security administration, Colonel Tomic and this other senior officer who was present when I was talking with them were familiar with many of the details that I knew. At that time I wasn't an active member of the Army of Yugoslavia. What I discussed with him he dictated in his own words into the record. At that time I did not think that being precise at any time or at any moment would be questioned of that statement or that I would have to then say whether I said that specific word or not. So I would like to ask you. I state that I saw people walking towards the buses. I cannot say the most logical conclusion would be that perhaps I saw the odd one going in. I know people were going into a part of the bus. I know they did have the option to choose where they wanted to go, whether to Croatia or to Serbia. Any -- each detail that you would like me to say, I'm really doing my utmost. And it's been a full 15 years since those events started, and in my life when I left the army I tried to forget all the ugly things that happened to me. I cannot for the moment answer. Anything that I would tell you, other than what I have said, would be some sort of a speculation or a conclusion on my part. So if I were to tell you -- what I mean is if I was looking at those people, the most logical thing would be that they were boarding the buses. Whether at that point in time I saw any of them entering the buses, perhaps I did see that, but anything further that I would say about that would be guessing or speculation. And that is something that I do not wish to do here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said that you were there with other Guards Brigade officers. What other Guards Brigade officers were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't often have the opportunity to meet Colonel Pavkovic. At one point in time he was an officer from the highest-ranking command, and I knew exactly who he was. I remember seeing him there. There were other officers, too. As far as I remember, Major Tesic was present, too. Members of the military police were there, too, but I can't be more specific. I wish -- I wish I could remember, but I can't. If you'd be so kind, please, as to point me to a situation that might jog my memory, perhaps then I'd be able to tell you whether it's something that I remember or not. Things being what they are, I'm now unable to do that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's try something you said yesterday on page 71. Your answer is: "I claim with the greatest of responsibility that at that moment none of my soldiers were present, either in the hospital or in the hospital compound around the hospital." Sir, if you didn't enter that hospital on November 20th or walk through the compound, how can you guarantee that none of your soldiers were inside or on the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, that morning all of my soldiers, all of my squad leaders, all of my company officers received an assignment from me directly to search the entire area along our own axis. All of my soldiers were instructed to pick up any weapons, equipment, ammunition, protective masks and helmets found there, or anything else that could be defined as combat or non-combat equipment. I personally told them to go and do that. I personally appointed squad leaders and told them where to go. I personally -- well, it's hard to verbalise this, but I think I told (redacted) at one point in time what he was supposed to be doing. What this means is my soldiers didn't have -- after that I went back to the town. I went back to the hospital. It is my deepest conviction that they could not have possibly got there at the time when I was there. There had been no time. They had their own commitments and assignments. At no point in time was I actually informed by anyone about any of my soldiers being or indeed needing to be at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, you can just offer your judgement, your personal judgement. You can't state for sure that none of your soldiers were inside because you can't tell if someone disobeyed your orders and was inside.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. I did not come across any of my soldiers in the hospital compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my deepest conviction --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Please continue. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my deepest conviction that the military police would not have allowed anyone uninvited to enter the hospital itself. Why then would they have allowed any soldier they didn't know, any officer they didn't know if this officer or soldier had no place being there in the first place? My personal inference follows. My soldiers simply had no time to get to the hospital, to reach the hospital compound, let alone to enter the hospital building itself or take any action inside it. I am convinced that none of them were inside the hospital building or, indeed, within the compound at the same time that I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you see Vukasinovic there? He's indicated in his statement that he was present at the hospital on that date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't for the life of me remember. I've known who Mr. Vukasinovic is for a very long time, but I cannot at all remember meeting him at any time or talking to him, or seeing him in any of those situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: What about Karanfilov, did you see him at the hospital on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Captain Karanfilov was a fellow student at the military academy, a fellow student of mine. We go back to our time at the military gymnasium. I don't remember seeing him at the hospital at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin, did you see him at the hospital on November 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember a single situation that would now jog my memory. I've heard many stories about his presence there, here in this courtroom, but I can't remember seeing him there. He may have passed me at some point, but even for me this was -- well, not exactly interesting situation but I really don't remember seeing him. This might have been the ordinary situation, so ordinary in fact as to leave me unable to even remember it. I apologise. I do remember Colonel Pavkovic because he was an officer that I did not exactly get to see every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many officers did you see at the hospital on that morning of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, my impression is that there were a great many officers there on the 20th. There was quite a crowd there. There was a general sense of commotion and confusion. It's difficult to name names. I did like to know, as I indicated yesterday, what became of certain people that I used to know. But I think at one point in time I may have even exchanged greetings with some of those officers, but I can't for the life of me remember their names right now. I regret to have to say this, I sincerely do, but that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you able to determine who was in charge, sir, while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say one thing. I didn't get the impression at the time that this was some sort of an operation. My impression at the time was that the crowd there, the civilians, were perfectly free to say what they would like to do and to go wherever they chose. I didn't understand why the need would ever arise to begin with. I know that the town had been disarmed. I personally witnessed all of that. I saw this with my very own eyes. I saw what Vukovar was like, and I didn't believe that people could continue to live in a place like that. I thought that's why everybody was leaving and not because somebody was actually forcing them to leave. I didn't see this as an operation where people were being shifted and sent this way or that. I'm telling you my impression at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, you don't know who was in charge. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I was not aware of the fact that there had been an evacuation there previously, nor was I trying to find out at the time, honestly. I thought everything was going according to plan, some plan devised by someone back at the superior command. I thought there was no need for me to interfere, nor indeed was I in a position to interfere with something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, witness 16 places you at the hospital while people are being taken away and speaks to you. And he said you were upset over a number of soldiers being killed, and you referred to the prisoners who were being taken away as dead men. How did you know prisoners were going to be killed, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Firstly, given the serious nature of this situation, the statement itself is so illogical, so biased. Firstly, I find it to be illogical, and as soon as this was uttered, I realised that I was now being pushed into a situation where I had to start hating someone, where I had to start wishing evil upon someone, whereas eventually it turns out that this person had never even experienced that. If indeed I was an eye-witness to this, as this witness seems to be claiming, as far as I have so far heard over the course of this trial, those people who left in the ambulances came to no harm at all. I really don't know what the reasons are driving this gentleman to tout this story to anyone and to offend me like that, as a human being. I don't think I have ever been in a situation where the look in my eyes might freeze anyone. I don't think I don't know what this means at all, a freezing glance. I myself never caught myself in a situation where I said that people walking past me were dead just because I was wishing them dead and then nothing happens in the end. You see what I'm saying. I claim with the utmost responsibility for this honourable Trial Chamber that this scene never took place, as described by the gentleman. And I think the reference here is to witness P016. I tried hard to understand what his motives might be, but I have so far failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you know of no motive for him to lie about you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That person claimed he knew me from before, that he wrote to my unit when we were at Pasuljanske Livade which is a training camp that JNA units sometimes would be sent to. You have Mr. Mrksic here who was the commander of the Guards Brigade at the time. You have the then-Major Sljivancanin, who was chief of security. There will be other officers coming. If any one of them ever says that they went to Pasuljanske Livade and that I was there, well I am telling you, I assure you that I have never in my life been to Pasuljanske Livade, that I have never spoken to this gentleman, that he has never laid eyes on me in his entire life, and that I never found myself in the situation that he described within the hospital compound -- or rather, outside the gate. There are no steps outside the door, as he described. No scene like that ever took place. I am telling you what this man said is a total fabrication. I don't know what might have driven him to do anything like that. I suppose a large-scale fabrication of that nature takes a lot of courage, which I don't think I would ever be able to summon up myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. Seselj visited in November of 1991, and he went to the house where you were staying, that same house that was being used as your observation post. Were you aware that Seselj was going to be visiting your observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I associate Seselj's arrival with a particular situation, if I may be allowed to give you just a short account of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, there's a question. Were you aware that Seselj was visiting your post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. What this means is Seselj was never in the house in my presence, the house that I used as an observation post, the house in which I was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. You said he was never in your presence. Were you aware that he was visiting -- going to visit that observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see any reason for him to be visiting my observation post at all, nor did any of my subordinates ever inform me of the fact that he had been there. I also wish to point out something else. The day he visited Vukovar I had been preparing to leave for Belgrade, and the next day -- as a matter of fact, I spent that entire day in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were never made aware on that day or the next day that Seselj visited your observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We had a Defence witness, Jaksic, who said he saw Seselj's secretary present at your observation post. Were you aware that Seselj's secretary was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea who Seselj's secretary is, and I certainly don't know that Mr. Jaksic ever came to my observation post. He was perfectly entitled to come, but I simply never saw him there, nor did I ever hear of him coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness 018 testified that you were present at that apartment/observation post when Seselj visited. Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness P018 said a lot of things that I wish to deny, what you have just indicated being one of the many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness P022 stated that you were present at your apartment/observation post when Seselj visited. Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Witness P002, who seems to have no ties to 018 or 022, has testified that you were present in your apartment/observation post when Seselj visited and that he placed this information in his diary. Do you deny that too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is there anything linking P002 and P022? I think the witness himself, P022, said that at one point they were back in his own native place, as far as I remember, and please correct me if I'm wrong. The way they both described this, at least in my understanding, involves a lot of discrepancy. Witness P002 wrote down in his notebook a number of different things and stated before this Chamber things that couldn't be further from the truth or further from evidence which I myself found in his notebook. I assure you that I was never in the situation described by witness P002, and the scene simply never took place involving Seselj and the officers which he named or, indeed, the circumstances that he described. If you can allow me to show you all of this on the sketch that I used to indicate certain things to the Trial Chamber yesterday, I can explain in very simple terms why this would not have been feasible to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, after the break. Let me just finish asking you some questions. You can show that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will now adjourn. There must be a redaction, so we'll resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Let us continue with the Seselj meeting. Do you know which -- did you learn which of your soldiers or subordinates were present for that meeting that occurred at your observation post with Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I claim that this meeting did not take place at my observation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that Seselj made some remarks at your observation point or elsewhere that not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I heard this statement was here at the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you weren't at your home and observation point on November 13th, as you state, you cannot state for sure whether or not Seselj was there. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, as far as I am able to understand, Seselj did not have a single reason to come to a house. If I were in that house, if I resided at their house but was not present there. And I can tell you that no one ever told me that meetings were ever held in that house at any point, and that is why I state that no meeting was held there of the kind described in some evidence before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So no one has every told you that and you weren't there, according to your testimony. Sir, if someone -- or let's say Seselj, who was a noted politician in the former Yugoslavia, makes statements of that kind to troops that no Ustasha is allowed to leave alive, is that a dangerous situation when something like that is made to troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, at that time -- in fact, throughout my military career I was not politically involved. At one point, along with perhaps a hundred -- almost a hundred per cent of the officers in the JNA, I was in the communist party --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but when the League of Communists of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, there is a question. When a statement like that is made from a politician, is that a dangerous situation? We don't need your whole political history what you did with other officers. It's a question. Can you answer the question, please. When a statement like that is made, is that a dangerous situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So your claim that Seselj was a famous politician is something that I do not share. I did not see him as a famous politician at all, but I allow that somebody else might think that. But any attempts to lure somebody to do evil is potentially a dangerous situation. If he really did say at one point that no Ustasha should be allowed to leave Vukovar alive, that's something that I don't know about. I did not witness that. If this is something that he said, then you should ask him or people who were present when he made that statement. Such a sentence uttered by a politician of this kind would not have any effect on me whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you know within one week of that statement being uttered, over 200 people were killed. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is your claim. So I cannot accept that since I -- because I did not witness when this statement was made, I cannot now say whether this motivated anyone to do anything; it did not motivate me. Nor had I known about this statement -- had I known about it at all, I'm sure that I personally would have taken measures to prevent anything like that. But I absolutely did not know about this statement, and it is an insult for me when somebody says that I had known about it and that I took it just like that without doing anything, with equanimity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you took no action because you didn't know about it. Are you aware of anyone who took any action after that statement was made, any action taken by anyone in the military?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's too obvious, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Withdrawn, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought your client -- on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to a few other issues quickly. Sir, you testified yesterday that between November 10th and November 19th you provided security for homes in two neighbourhoods, and you mentioned Bosko Buha and I think Milovo Brdo. Is that correct, sir? That's on page 57 of yesterday's testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the line that we had reached according to the last task that I received from my commander. When we reached the line at Milovo Brdo, my troops remained there to secure a part of Milovo Brdo and of the Bosko Buha settlement. So what you said is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, were you involved in -- was your company involved in combat operations after November 10th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think I was quite clear. My company had two combat missions. The first was to come to the 6th Proleterske Division settlement and the second was to reach the Milovo Brdo settlement. My company and myself, we did not receive any other combat missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you and your company were carrying out combat missions right through the end of November 17th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you take it to mean that one of the combat missions was to secure the line that had been reached, then I agree with you. But missions that would involve attacking, I say that the assault detachment did have such tasks, but I personally did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, your company, was it carrying out combat operations - and you know what combat operations are - after November 10th? Isn't it true it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to correct you. A company cannot perform combat operations. A company is assigned its axis of action, and this is the lowest unit of permanent composition. I have to apologise stressing this, but I think a misuse of those terms actually resulted in this confusion whether I am a commander or a leader, whether I was engaged in operations or in actions, because a company cannot perform combat operations. A company is given a combat task and it has to carry it out on a given axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir, isn't it true that your company was carrying out combat operations along a certain axis or direction right up until November 17th, 1991? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to repeat. My company --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- carried out its combat task.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, please state yes or no. If you disagree, please let us know, but not a long statement repeating over and over your views on life. Were you carrying out combat operations up until November 17th, 1991? If it's no, it's fine, if it's yes, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never performed combat operations, "operacija" in B/C/S. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown his first statement. In English 03054580 through 82; in B/C/S it is 02188354, and that particular page. The middle of the page just below "statement." In English it's page 1, Your Honours. It's page 8354 in B/C/S. The seventh line down in the middle -- or actually you can go to the sixth line, one above. Starting: "I received all orders for the preparation ..." Do you see that, sir, sixth line down after "statement."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. "I received all orders for the preparation and the execution of combat operations from the two of them. My company was carrying out combat operations in the direction of Petrova Gora settlement-Seste Proleterske division, settlement, as far as the Vuka River. Along the Vuka River towards the Dunav," and it says Danube Hotel, "which was situated at the mouth of the Vuka into the Danube. The right border of my company was Promaska Street. My company reached the Danube River in the afternoon hours on 17 November when the active combat operations of my battalion ceased." Is that what that says there, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've told the security organ in 1998 that you were performing combat operations up until November 17th, when active combat operations of the battalion ceased. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And today and yesterday you said that you weren't performing combat operations, and the reason for that change, sir, is that you don't want those troops still resubordinated to you, the troops that committed the murders. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's entirely wrong. If you allow I will explain. We keep talking about the battalion now, and to this day, I accept that the 1st Battalion was my unit. I was a member, a soldier, of that unit. I was not a commander of the 1st Battalion, but the Guards Brigade was the unit that I belonged to, that was my unit. Let me just say here that my company was engaged in combat along the axis of Petrova Gora-Seste Proleterske settlements. This is an axis; it's an imaginary axis. And I said many times that I had two tasks. The first task was to reach the Seste Proleterske settlement and the next one was to reach the Milovo Brdo settlement. And if somebody says differently, then please tell me, where.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, your commander, Mr. Tesic, says the same thing, that your axis was that south-east of the hospital and that the battalion finished its combat operations at the end of the 17th, which is consistent with your statement, sir, that combat operations ended on the 17th. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I have already said once before that the assault detachment, Major Tesic -- when my unit reached the Milovo Brdo area, up until that time he visited my area only once. And after that time, he was at Milovo Brdo every day and he was present at the rest of the axis where the assault detachment was active. I didn't want and I couldn't control what he was doing every day, to stand behind his shoulder. But he was a responsible, serious officer, and he knew what he was doing. And if the assault detachment was supposed to do those things, then this was probably in accordance with the orders that he himself received from Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your statements and the summaries that were filed by your attorneys to this Court, in no place does it say that you stopped combat operations on November 10th. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never saw the summaries submitted by my Defence team. I doubt that they actually wrote something to that effect because they have been aware of my defence -- what I intend to use in my defence all along from the start. In my statement given to the military court in 1998, I said quite clearly that I finished with my task at Milovo Brdo. Please check, and if I'm wrong, tell me so. Show me where it says that I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said in your statement, in the first statement, that: "My company reached the Danube River in the afternoon hours on 17 November when active combat operations of my battalion ceased." Your company was still active in combat operations until November 17th; that's what you said. Are you now saying something different, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. You present this in a wrong way. In the statement that you now show me it says that my unit reached the Danube River on the 17th of November in the afternoon hours when the active combat ended within my battalion. I still maintain that I am a -- I was a member of the 1st Motorised Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the active combat of that -- operations of that battalion ceased on that day, just as yours did, too, when you reached the Danube. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not reach the Danube River. I say again that my last combat task was completed at the time when I took Milovo Brdo. I did come to the Danube River and to the Dunav Hotel after the fall of Vukovar, but this does not mean that my actions resulted in this. It is my statement that Major Borivoj Tesic commanded the actions from Milovo Brdo until the 17th of December when the units, certain units, reached the Dunav Hotel. If anyone says anything different, please show me that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said: "My company reached the Danube River." You just said on page 98, line 10: "I did not reach the Danube River." I did not put that in the statement. Sir, you signed that statement, didn't you, in 1998? You signed that statement in 1998, didn't you, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you persistently that in the statement that you are showing me says that my unit reached the Danube River on the 17th of November in the afternoon, when the active combat ended in my battalion. I did not mention the company anywhere, did I?
